topic: International Trade and the Global Economy
subject: economics

items.title: Potential GDP is not directly observable
items.claim: The output gap is actual GDP minus potential GDP, expressed as a percentage of potential. Why is this concept difficult to use in practice?

options.text: Potential GDP is unobservable — it must be estimated, and estimates are revised heavily after the fact. Pre-2008 estimates of potential GDP have been revised down substantially, suggesting the economy was less overheated than thought
It is observable directly from satellite

items.reveal_title: A concept whose measurement is treacherous
items.reveal:
OECD, IMF and central bank estimates of potential GDP use filters (Hodrick-Prescott, Kalman) and production function approaches. They produce different numbers and revise heavily as data arrives.

Orphanides's 2003 paper showed that real-time output gap estimates available to the Fed in the 1970s were systematically wrong, contributing to policy errors.

The BIS has criticised reliance on output gaps for monetary policy.
items.why: Policy variables that depend on unobservable concepts inherit estimation uncertainty. Output gap-based 'rules' look cleaner in textbooks than in practice.

items.title: Tulip mania was less extreme than the legend
items.claim: Charles Mackay's 1841 'Extraordinary Popular Delusions' painted 17th-century Dutch tulip mania as a society-wide frenzy that crashed the economy. What does modern research find?

options.text: The crash bankrupted the Dutch Republic for a generation

Trading was confined largely to a small group of professional florists meeting in taverns; while bulb prices rose sharply and crashed in February 1637, the macro impact was modest and Mackay's tales of devastated cobblers are mostly unverified
Tulip mania never happened; it is a complete fabrication
It triggered the Eighty Years' War

items.reveal_title: A bubble, but a smaller one
items.reveal:
Anne Goldgar's 'Tulipmania' (2007) used archival records to show that bulb trading was largely among well-off merchants, that few contracts were ever actually enforced after the February 1637 crash, and that contemporary Calvinist moral pamphlets exaggerated the social ruin for didactic purposes.

Peter Garber argued similarly from an economist's perspective: peak prices for rare bulbs may have reflected genuine scarcity and fashion premiums, not pure delusion.

Mackay's account was readable, lurid and influential — but not historical.
items.why: Pop economic history is full of morality tales. The actual record is usually messier and less satisfying — but it's what students of bubbles need to grapple with.

items.title: Dutch disease named for Netherlands natural gas
items.claim: The 'Dutch disease' concept emerged from observing the Netherlands after its 1959 Groningen natural gas discovery. What's the mechanism?

options.text: Resource exports appreciate the real exchange rate, making non-resource tradable sectors (manufacturing) uncompetitive; when the resource is exhausted or prices fall, the diminished manufacturing base struggles to recover
Resource discovery always raises GDP permanently

items.reveal:
The Economist coined the term in 1977. Corden and Neary (1982) formalised the mechanism in a two-sector model with traded and non-traded goods.

Observed cases: Netherlands itself (1960s-70s); Venezuela's oil dependence; Nigeria; arguably the UK in the North Sea oil era. Counter-examples (Norway's sovereign wealth fund) show institutional design can mitigate the effect.

The broader 'resource curse' literature (Sachs and Warner, Acemoglu and others) extends to institutional and political channels.
items.why: Natural resource booms are mixed blessings. The institutional and macroeconomic management determines whether they fund long-run development or undermine it.
